## A6. Technical notes

\applabel{A6}{app:technical-notes}This section explains two results reported in the body of this chapter: the growth with $\tau$ of the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, and the rise with $\tau$ of the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity. The stored results keep neither $\hat\rho$ nor the standard error of each fit, so we re-ran every block for the six designs, both neighbor types, and all five values of $\tau$, 2.4 million fits of the oracle model, recording $\hat\rho$ and the standard error, and the re-run reproduced the stored results in all 9,600 scenarios. Numbers below that involve $\hat\rho$, the standard error, or the terms of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} come from this re-run; the others come from the stored results.

### Estimation error and its dependence on $\tau$

For one fit $(k, j)$, write $Y$, $Z$, and $\epsilon$ for $Y_{kj}$, $Z_{kj}$, and $\epsilon_{kj}$ (Simulation design, resampling, and metrics). Let $V = [1, Z, S(Z), X_k]$ be the $100 \times 4$ covariate matrix of the oracle model, so that Equation \ref{eq:outcome} reads $(I - \rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon$ with $\theta = (0, \tau, 1, \beta)^\top$. Let $A = (I - \rho W)^{-1}$ and $V^{+} = (V^\top V)^{-1}V^\top$, and for a vector $v$ write $[V^{+}v]_Z$ for the coefficient on $Z$ when $v$ is regressed on the columns of $V$ by least squares. Given $\hat\rho$, the estimated coefficients are $V^{+}(I - \hat\rho W)Y$ (Estimation). Because $(I - \hat\rho W)Y = V\theta + \epsilon + (\rho - \hat\rho)WY$ and $WY = WA(V\theta + \epsilon)$,
\begin{equation}
\hat\tau - \tau = [V^{+}\epsilon]_Z + (\rho - \hat\rho)\,h + \tau(\rho - \hat\rho)\,g, \label{eq:error-decomposition}
\end{equation}
where
$$
g = [V^{+}WAZ]_Z, \qquad h = [V^{+}WA\{S(Z) + \beta X_k + \epsilon\}]_Z.
$$
The first term has mean zero given $Z$ and $X_k$. The last term carries a factor of $\tau$. It is present exactly when $g \neq 0$, where $g$ is the coefficient on $Z$ when the lagged treatment $WAZ = WZ + \rho W^2 Z + \rho^2 W^3 Z + \cdots$ is regressed on the model's own covariates, and its sign and size are set by the error in $\hat\rho$. The concentrated likelihood depends on $Y$ only through the residual sum of squares of $(I - \tilde\rho W)Y$ on $V$, and the part of that residual that involves $\tau$ is $\tau(\rho - \tilde\rho)$ times the residual of $WAZ$ on $V$. If $WAZ$ lies in the column space of $V$, that part vanishes for every $\tilde\rho$, so $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$; if in addition $g = 0$, then $\hat\tau - \tau$ is the same at every value of $\tau$. Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} held on every re-run fit, with a largest residual of $4.2\times10^{-13}$; for Checkerboard under rook contiguity it held in the reduced form given below.

Two consequences of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} explain the results for $\tau$ reported in the body.

First, for designs whose treated clusters have treated neighbors, the last term gives a small positive bias that grows with $\tau$. Under queen contiguity, pooled over the 160 blocks, the bias of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants rose from 0.029 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.047 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), while that of Isolation Buffer stayed between 0.002 and 0.004. Almost all of the rise is the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition}. In our fits, $\hat\rho$ was biased downward by about 0.06 on average (for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, by 0.071 at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.054 at $\tau = 3$). We observed this downward bias in these simulations; we did not derive it or check it against a published finite-sample result. With $\rho - \hat\rho$ positive on average, the last term is positive and grows with $\tau$ for any design with $g > 0$. For Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, $g$ averaged 0.371 over the queen fits, and the last term contributed 0.021 of the bias at $\tau = 0.8$ and 0.043 at $\tau = 3$; the first term contributed 0.001 at both values, and the second 0.007 and 0.002. For Isolation Buffer, $g$ averaged 0.020, and the last term contributed 0.001 and 0.004. Most of the difference in $g$ comes from the control-only regime. Under the both-arms regime with $\rho = 0$, the lagged treatment is $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma$, one of the covariates, so $g = 0$ for every design. Under the control-only regime, $WZ = S(Z)/\gamma + Z \circ WZ$, and at $\rho = 0$, $g$ is close to the average share of treated neighbors among treated clusters. That share is 0.57 for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, whose treated clusters are concentrated in the high-saturation quadrants, and exactly 0 for Isolation Buffer, whose treated clusters have no treated neighbors. For Isolation Buffer, $Z \circ WZ = 0$, so the two regimes define the same spillover covariate and the same $g$, which is 0 at $\rho = 0$ and about 0.06 at $\rho = 0.5$; at $\rho = 0$, its $\hat\rho$ and its estimation error were the same at every value of $\tau$, up to the optimizer's tolerance.

The same term explains why the control-only MSE of Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants rose from 0.131 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.182 at $\tau = 3$ while that of Isolation Buffer did not. Under that regime, averaged over the 80 queen blocks, the variance of the last term of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} rose from 0.008 to 0.061 for Incidence-Guided Saturation Quadrants, while the variance of the rest of the error changed little (0.119 and 0.115). The variance of the last term grew more slowly than $\tau^2$ because $\hat\rho$ became less variable as $\tau$ grew. For Isolation Buffer, the variance of the last term stayed below 0.0002. The rise in bias slowed at larger values of $\tau$ for a related reason: the part of the likelihood that involves $\tau$ sharpens it around the true $\rho$ as $\tau$ grows, so the downward bias of $\hat\rho$ shrank.

Second, the decomposition explains why the coverage of Checkerboard under rook contiguity rose with $\tau$. Under rook contiguity, Checkerboard's coverage rose from 0.138 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.442 at $\tau = 3$ (Stability across treatment effect sizes), although its coefficient on $Z$ estimates $\tau - \gamma$ at every value of $\tau$. For this design $WZ = 1 - Z$, and because $W$ is row-standardized, $W^2 Z = W(1 - Z) = Z$. The powers of $W$ applied to $Z$ therefore alternate between $1 - Z$ and $Z$, and $WAZ = \{(1 - Z) + \rho Z\}/(1 - \rho^2)$ lies in the span of the intercept and $Z$. The derivation of Equation \ref{eq:error-decomposition} applies with the aliased spillover column dropped, $V = [1, Z, X_k]$ and $\theta = (\gamma, \tau - \gamma, \beta)^\top$, so that $\tau - \gamma$ takes the place of $\tau$, and $g = -1/(1 + \rho)$. Two consequences follow: $\hat\rho$ is the same at every value of $\tau$, and
$$
\hat\tau - \tau = -\gamma + \delta + (\tau - \gamma)\,\frac{\hat\rho - \rho}{1 + \rho},
$$
where $\delta$ collects the first two terms of that decomposition and, like $\hat\rho$, does not depend on $\tau$. The error in $\hat\rho$ is therefore multiplied by $\tau - \gamma$, which grows with $\tau$. The mean standard deviation of $\hat\tau$ rose from 0.202 at $\tau = 0.8$ to 0.327 at $\tau = 3$, and the standard error tracked it, rising on average from 0.199 to 0.322. With the bias held near $-\gamma$, wider intervals covered $\tau$ more often. The rise was largest at $\rho = 0$ (coverage 0.145 to 0.541) and smallest at $\rho = 0.5$ (0.130 to 0.265), consistent with the factor $1/(1 + \rho)$. The same term raised the MSE from 0.477 to 0.567. About three quarters of that increase was variance, $(n-1)\text{SD}^2/n$ averaged over scenarios (Appendix \ref{app:mechanics}), which rose from 0.041 to 0.109. The other quarter was squared bias, which rose from 0.436 to 0.458 because $\hat\rho$ was biased slightly downward, moving the mean bias from $-0.650$ to $-0.667$. The higher coverage at large $\tau$ reflects wider intervals around the wrong quantity, not a recovery of $\tau$.
